1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4.name: English Opening: Anglo-Indian Defence, King's Knight Variation
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4.background: The same position arises from 1.c4 Nf6 2.Nf3. The English Opening is named after Howard Staunton, who played 1.c4 in his 1843 match against Saint-Amant and at London 1851, the first international tournament, but it caught on only in the twentieth century.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e6.strategy: Opens the f8-bishop's diagonal and prepares ...d5, keeping every set-up open: Black can still choose between a classical centre and a set-up with a fianchettoed bishop. The cost is the c8-bishop, which the e6-pawn shuts in until ...b6 gives it the long diagonal.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6.name: English Opening: Anglo-Indian Defence, King's Indian Formation
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6.background: Until the mid-1930s the King's Indian Defence was generally regarded as highly suspect, but the analysis and play of three Soviet players in particular, Alexander Konstantinopolsky, Isaac Boleslavsky and David Bronstein, helped to make it much more respected and popular.
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6.strategy: Prepares ...Bg7 and quick castling, and leaves open whether Black strikes in the centre at once or builds up slowly. The cost is the centre: Black lets White occupy it first and relies on undermining it later with pawn breaks.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c5.name: English Opening: Symmetrical Variation
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c5.background: The same position arises from 1.c4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6. The Hedgehog Defence, a line of it, continues 3.g3 b6 4.Bg2 Bb7 5.Nc3 e6 6.O-O Be7 7.d4 cxd4 8.Qxd4 d6; the ideas behind the Hedgehog were originally developed in the English Opening, and it first became extensively analysed in the 1970s.
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c5.strategy: Controls d4, just as White's c-pawn controls d5, so White cannot take the centre for free. The cost is space: if White gets e4 in beside c4, Black's position is cramped and needs freeing breaks such as ...d5. The game is usually a manoeuvring fight over d4 and d5.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 b6.name: English Opening: Anglo-Indian Defence, Queen's Indian Formation
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 b6.background: The Queen's Indian Defence, a solid defence to the Queen's Pawn Game, takes its name from the fianchetto of Black's queen's bishop and is regarded as the sister opening of the Nimzo-Indian.
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7, which adds to the f6-knight's control of e4 and d5 and claims the long diagonal. Black puts no pawn in the centre yet and controls it from a distance, which leaves White the choice of structure.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 d5.name: English Opening: Anglo-Indian Defence, Scandinavian Defence
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 d5.strategy: Challenges c4 at once. If White takes on d5, Black's knight has moved twice while White builds a centre with pawns. It is sound, but White chooses the structure.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 with a Slav-type pawn chain that keeps the c8-bishop's diagonal open to develop outside the pawns. It is sound but passive, and the b8-knight loses c6 and usually develops via d7.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 d6.name: English Opening: Anglo-Indian Defence, Old Indian Formation
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 d6.background: Siegbert Tarrasch introduced the Old Indian Defence in 1902, but it is more commonly associated with Mikhail Chigorin, who adopted it five years later and pioneered it late in his career. It is considered sound but has never attained the popularity of the King's Indian.
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 d6.strategy: Prepares ...e5 and opens the c8-bishop's diagonal, a modest set-up that can still turn into a fianchetto of the king's bishop. It is sound, but White can build a broad centre, and if the f8-bishop ends up on e7 rather than g7 Black is usually cramped.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 Nc6.strategy: Develops the knight and keeps a central pawn advance in reserve, but the knight on c6 blocks the c-pawn and rules out ...c5 and ...c6. It is sound but less flexible than the main moves.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 Na6.strategy: Puts the second knight on the rim, heading for b4 or c5, where it does nothing for the centre. White builds the centre at leisure.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 a6.strategy: Prepares ...b5 against the c4-pawn but spends a tempo on a rook's pawn instead of developing a second piece. White builds the centre at leisure, and once the knight is on c3 the push ...b5 costs a pawn.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 a5.strategy: Restrains b4 but spends a tempo on a rim pawn, weakens b5 and fights neither for the centre nor for development. White continues at leisure.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 b5.strategy: Offers the b-pawn for queenside pressure, but without a White pawn on d5 and without ...c5 to open the queenside. After 3.cxb5 White keeps the extra pawn, and the pressure on the queenside does not make up for it.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 h6.strategy: Takes g5 from White's pieces but spends a tempo on a rim pawn without developing anything or touching the centre. White continues undisturbed.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 h5.strategy: Supports a knight on g4 and prepares ...h4, but develops nothing and gives up ...h6 as a way to cover g5. White uses the free tempo to develop.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 Ng8.strategy: Returns the knight to g8 and undoes Black's only developing move. With c4 and Nf3 already played, White is two tempi ahead and can take the centre as it likes.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 Ng4.strategy: Moves the knight a second time without a real threat, since the king guards f2 and the rook guards h2. After 3.h3 it has to retreat, and Black has lost time that White uses for the centre.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 Nh5.strategy: Moves the knight a second time to the rim, where it no longer covers d5 or e4. White builds the centre while the knight on h5 takes no part in the fight for it.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 Ne4.strategy: Moves the knight a second time to e4, where no pawn supports it. 3.d3 drives it away at once, and White gains time for the centre.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 Rg8.strategy: Gives up kingside castling for good and develops nothing, since the rook has no work on g8. White builds the centre while Black's king can at best castle long.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e5.strategy: Leaves the pawn en prise: 3.Nxe5 wins it, and Black has no real compensation, since White keeps the pawn and simply develops.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g5.strategy: Hangs the g-pawn, which the f3-knight attacks and nothing defends, since the e7-pawn blocks the queen's diagonal. After 3.Nxg5 White is a pawn up and Black's kingside is loosened for nothing.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 Nd5.strategy: Hangs the knight: 3.cxd5 wins it outright, since the d7-pawn blocks the queen from recapturing and nothing else covers d5.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight to the square that watches d5 and e4, so Black's own central advance is hard to achieve. White keeps the central advance in reserve and plays for a lasting, slight initiative in a mirror-image pawn structure where both sides hold the same flank pawns.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.b4.name: English Opening: Symmetrical Variation, Napolitano Gambit
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.b4.strategy: Offers a flank pawn at once, hoping to deflect Black's c-pawn from the centre and win queenside activity. Black simply takes it with ...cxb4 and is a pawn up, and White's compensation is thin, since only the f3-knight is developed to make use of the open lines.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d4.strategy: Challenges the c5 pawn at once. The usual exchange leaves White's knight centralised on d4 and gives Black a half-open c-file against the c4 pawn; White gets more space and the more active pieces, at the price of the flexibility of a slow set-up.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.g3.strategy: Fianchettoes the king's bishop to bear on the long diagonal and the centre from a distance, and delays the central advance. White plays a slow, flexible game for a lasting small edge, with the choice of pushing in the centre kept for later.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6 3.b3.strategy: Supports the c4 pawn and prepares the bishop on the long diagonal. White leaves the d-pawn at home, preferring to see how Black declares the centre and then to fight for d5 with pieces from a distance, in the manner of a flexible flank opening.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6 3.g3.strategy: Prepares the fianchetto of the king's bishop, aimed down the long diagonal at the d5 square that Black's c6 pawn is about to claim. White keeps the central advance in reserve and plays for slow pressure; the price is that Black may build a broad centre first.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6 3.d4.strategy: Takes the centre at once and steers the game into a solid structure in which Black's c6 pawn backs a pawn on d5. White gets more space and a clear, well-mapped game, but spends the flexibility of the flank approach.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight toward d5 and e4 and keeps every pawn plan open. If Black claims the centre, White can trade, build up solidly or fight for the centre, with the knight already placed. A natural, flexible move that delays the commitment.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6 3.b3 d5.strategy: Takes the centre at once with a pawn that c6 already supports, and hits the c4 pawn. White's b3 holds it, so the tension is stable, and Black gets a solid structure and a clear claim to the centre.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6 3.b3 e6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 with a second pawn behind it and builds a compact, safe centre; the king's bishop gets its diagonal. The cost is the light-squared bishop, which the e6 pawn blocks on its natural diagonal and which has to find another way out later.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6 3.b3 g6.strategy: Prepares ...Bg7 so that Black's bishop meets White's on the long diagonal. A sound, patient set-up that gives White time to take more space, since Black spends moves on the kingside before the centre is settled.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6 3.b3 d5 4.Bb2.strategy: Completes the fianchetto: the bishop eyes the long diagonal and the kingside, while the b3 pawn keeps c4 defended against the d5 pawn. White chooses piece pressure and flexibility over an immediate central advance, and awaits Black's plan for the light-squared bishop.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6 3.b3 d5 4.g3.strategy: Brings the king's bishop to the long diagonal, so that with the queen's bishop on b2 both aim at the centre and the queenside from a distance. The b3 pawn still holds c4, so White can leave the central tension as it is and keeps a flexible, patient set-up.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6 3.b3 d5 4.cxd5.strategy: Resolves the tension at once: if Black retakes with the c-pawn, the c-file is open to both sides and the game is level. It is solid, but it gives up the pressure on d5 that White's set-up is built on and leaves little to play for.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6 3.b3 d5 4.Bb2 Bf5.name: Réti Opening: Anglo-Slav Variation, New York System
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6 3.b3 d5 4.Bb2 Bf5.strategy: Develops the light-squared bishop outside the pawn chain while it still can, before ...e6 shuts it in, and eyes the b1-knight and the d3 square. Black gets an active piece for free and keeps a solid centre; the bishop may have to retreat later if White challenges it.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6 3.b3 d5 4.Bb2 Bg4.name: Réti Opening: Anglo-Slav Variation, Capablanca Variation
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6 3.b3 d5 4.Bb2 Bg4.strategy: Puts pressure on the f3-knight, which only the e- and g-pawns defend, and threatens to trade it and take away its control of e5 and d4. Black also gets the bishop out before ...e6, at the price of spending a move that White's pieces can try to use.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6 3.b3 d5 4.Bb2 e6.strategy: Supports d5 with a second pawn and builds a compact, safe centre; the king's bishop gets its diagonal. The cost is the light-squared bishop, which the e6 pawn blocks on its natural diagonal, so it is a long-term question how it gets out.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6 3.b3 d5 4.Bb2 g6.strategy: Prepares ...Bg7 so that Black's bishop meets White's on the long diagonal. A sound, patient set-up that gives White time to take more space, since Black spends moves on the kingside before the light-squared bishop and the centre are settled.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6 3.b3 d5 4.Bb2 Bf5 5.e3.name: Réti Opening: Anglo-Slav Variation, New York System
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6 3.b3 d5 4.Bb2 Bf5 5.e3.strategy: Opens the f1-bishop's diagonal and prepares quick castling in a solid set-up. White lets Black's bishop keep its active diagonal for now and decides the central plan later, preferring sound development to an early attempt to harass the bishop.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6 3.b3 d5 4.Bb2 Bf5 5.d3.name: Réti Opening: Anglo-Slav Variation, New York System
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6 3.b3 d5 4.Bb2 Bf5 5.d3.strategy: Cuts the f5-bishop's view of the b1-knight at d3 and covers e4, but the pawn on d3 also shuts the f1-bishop's diagonal, which has to come out by another route. A modest move that slows White's own development to reduce Black's activity.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6 3.b3 d5 4.Bb2 Bf5 5.g3.strategy: Fianchettoes the king's bishop, so that both bishops aim down the long diagonals at the centre, and leaves the f5-bishop alone. The b3 pawn keeps c4 defended, so White can develop without worrying about d5. A solid set-up for a slow, flexible game.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6 3.b3 d5 4.Bb2 Bg4 5.e3.name: Réti Opening: Anglo-Slav Variation, Capablanca Variation
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6 3.b3 d5 4.Bb2 Bg4 5.e3.strategy: Opens the f1-bishop's diagonal and prepares quick development. If Black trades on f3, the queen recaptures without damaging White's pawns. A solid, flexible answer that keeps the centre in reserve and leaves it to Black to decide whether to trade the bishop.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6 3.b3 d5 4.Bb2 Bg4 5.d3.name: Réti Opening: Anglo-Slav Variation, Capablanca Variation
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6 3.b3 d5 4.Bb2 Bg4 5.d3.strategy: Keeps the e-pawn flexible and supports a later central advance, but the pawn on d3 shuts the f1-bishop's diagonal, so that piece can come out only to e2 or after a kingside fianchetto. A modest set-up that develops more slowly than the alternative.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6 3.b3 d5 4.Bb2 Bg4 5.h3.strategy: Asks the g4-bishop what it wants at once. If Black trades on f3, White has to recapture with a pawn, since the e2 pawn blocks the queen: that costs doubled f-pawns but gives White the bishop pair and a half-open e-file. If the bishop retreats, h3 has taken g4 from it.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 d5 3.cxd5.strategy: Takes the pawn to clear the centre: the c-pawn is traded for Black's d-pawn, leaving White with d- and e-pawns against Black's single e-pawn in the middle. The game then turns on whether that central majority outweighs the activity Black's pieces gain.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 d5 3.d4.strategy: Claims the centre at once and lets the game settle into a solid queen's-pawn structure in which White keeps a small space advantage and Black must decide how to support d5 and when to release the tension. White keeps the pawns together and the position flexible.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 d5 3.g3.strategy: Prepares the fianchetto of the king's bishop and offers the c4 pawn: if Black takes it, White regains it with a queen check on a4 and plays on with a flexible set-up. White lets Black keep the centre and relies on piece play, a sound but modest choice.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 d5 3.cxd5 Nxd5.name: English Opening: Anglo-Indian Defence, Scandinavian Defence, Exchange Variation
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 d5 3.cxd5 Nxd5.strategy: Recaptures with the knight, which lands on the best central square and keeps the queen at home. Black has traded the d-pawn for White's c-pawn and plays for piece activity against White's central pawn majority, but must take care not to lose time when the knight is challenged.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 d5 3.cxd5 Qxd5.strategy: Recaptures with the queen, which White attacks at once with Nc3, so Black spends another move getting it out of the way. The position stays sound, but White gains time to develop and to build the centre at leisure.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 d5 3.cxd5 c6.strategy: Offers a pawn instead of recapturing, hoping for quick development and open lines after ...Nxc6. White simply takes it and is a pawn up, and Black's lead in development is not enough to pay for it.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3.strategy: Fianchettoes the king's bishop to work along the long diagonal and keeps the centre squares under watch from a distance. White holds back the d-pawn and stays flexible, accepting that Black may stake out the centre at once; the game becomes strategic rather than tactical.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops a piece to a square that watches d5 and e4 and keeps every pawn set-up open for later. The cost is that White lets Black choose the structure: a solid blocked centre, a symmetrical pawn formation or an attack on the knight are all available.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.b3.strategy: Prepares the queenside fianchetto, so the bishop will look down the long diagonal. But it does nothing for the centre or for d5, and Black can take the central squares at once and hit c4. Sound enough, yet Black reaches easy equality.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.b3 d5.strategy: Plants a pawn in the centre and attacks the c4 pawn at once, before White's bishop on b2 can bear on the long diagonal. Black gets a solid pawn pair and free development, so White has spent a move on the fianchetto without gaining central space.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.b3 b6.strategy: Answers the fianchetto with a fianchetto: the bishop on b7 will fight White's for e4 and d5 from a distance, with no pawn committed in the centre. A flexible, solid set-up, but Black leaves the c4 pawn alone and White can still take the centre with d4.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.b3 c5.strategy: Strikes at d4 first, so White cannot build a pawn centre there without a fight, and keeps the queen's bishop and the d-pawn free. The cost is a little space and time: White's bishop is coming to b2 and Black has to decide later how to develop.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 d5.strategy: Claims the centre at once and puts the c4 pawn to the question. White's fianchettoed bishop will lean on the d5 pawn and the queenside, so Black gets a solid pawn pair in return for a long game of pressure that White steers.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 b6.strategy: Answers the fianchetto with one of its own: the bishop on the long diagonal will contest the squares White's bishop wants, above all e4. Black leaves the centre to White for now and relies on controlling it from a distance, which asks for accurate timing later.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 a6.name: English Opening: Anglo-Indian Defence, Romanishin Variation
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 a6.strategy: A waiting move that prepares to hit the c4 pawn with the b-pawn. It develops nothing and does not contest the centre, so White has a free hand to finish development; the point is that the queenside advance can be played with tempo once the position allows.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 a6 4.Bg2.strategy: The natural development: the bishop takes the long diagonal, aimed at b7 and the a8 corner once the f3 knight steps aside, which makes the planned queenside advance awkward for Black. White simply finishes development and lets the slow move show.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 a6 4.d4.strategy: Takes the centre at once and leaves the bishop's development for later. Black's ...a6 is then a spare move, useful only for a later queenside advance, so White gets its pawn centre while Black has done little to prevent it.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 a6 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops a piece towards the centre and watches d5 and e4. Sound and flexible, but it gains nothing over the simple bishop move: Black can challenge the knight with ...Bb4 and trade it off to double White's pawns.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 a6 4.Bg2 b5.name: English Opening: Romanishin Gambit
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 a6 4.Bg2 b5.strategy: Offers a pawn: after cxb5 axb5 Black has an open a-file and queenside space, but the a8 rook stands on the bishop's diagonal with nothing guarding it, and one knight move from f3 uncovers the attack. Black has to spend time covering it; a sharp try that is easier to meet than to play.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 a6 4.Bg2 d5.strategy: Claims the centre and challenges the c4 pawn at once. White's bishop on g2 is blocked by its own knight on f3, so the slow ...a6 costs Black little: it is a spare move that can prepare a later ...b5, while Black's centre is already in place.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 a6 4.Bg2 c5.strategy: Fights for d4 and prepares to challenge White's centre from the flank. Black builds a flexible queenside structure in which ...a6 supports a later ...b5 against the c4 pawn, and the long diagonal is less dangerous while the f3 knight and the b7 pawn stand in the way.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 a6 4.Bg2 Be7.strategy: Develops the bishop and prepares to castle, keeping every pawn structure open. It is sound but passive: Black does nothing about the centre or the c4 pawn, and White gets time to set up the pawn centre.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 b6 4.Bg2.strategy: Completes the fianchetto: the bishop sits on the long diagonal where it presses on the centre and the queenside, and White can castle next. It fits the whole set-up, since Black's queenside fianchetto will meet it on the same diagonal.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 b6 4.d4.strategy: Puts a pawn in the centre at once, against the plan of controlling it from a distance. With the bishop still to arrive on g2, the game usually reaches the same position as the bishop move, only with the move order reversed.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 b6 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops a piece towards the centre and eyes d5 and e4, but commits the knight before White's centre is settled. Black can challenge it with ...Bb4, trading bishop for knight to double White's pawns, so the move is sound without making much of the fianchetto.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 b6 4.Bg2 Bb7.name: English Opening: Anglo-Indian Defence, Queen's Indian Formation
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 b6 4.Bg2 Bb7.strategy: The mirror move: the bishops face each other along the long diagonal with the f3 knight between them, and Black fights for e4 and d5 from a distance. A flexible, closed game follows in which neither side has yet fixed the centre.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 b6 4.Bg2 Be7.strategy: Develops the bishop and prepares to castle, and leaves the queen's bishop free to choose its square. A solid, flexible move; Black keeps the position closed and waits to see how White sets up the centre.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 b6 4.Bg2 c5.strategy: Stakes a claim to d4 and stops White from taking the centre cleanly. It commits a pawn before Black's pieces are developed, so White can choose how to answer it; sound, but less flexible than simply developing.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3.strategy: Fianchettoes the king's bishop against Black's own fianchetto set-up. The bishop eyes the long diagonal and the queenside, White keeps the d-pawn flexible, and the game is a strategic, manoeuvring one in which neither side has committed to a pawn centre yet.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.b4.name: English Orangutan
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.b4.strategy: A wing pawn thrust that grabs queenside space and prepares a bishop on the long diagonal. But the advanced pawn has no pawn support and can be attacked from the flank, and it loosens the c3 square. Offbeat and playable, not a way to fight for an advantage.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3.strategy: Brings the queen's knight toward the centre and eyes d5 and e4, leaving White free to build a classical pawn centre or to fianchetto later. The knight blocks the c-pawn and Black can answer with an early central strike, so White has to decide how much of the centre to claim.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.d4.strategy: Claims the centre at once and steers the game into the main King's Indian structure: White has the space, Black has to undermine the centre with pawn breaks and piece play. A natural way to take the lead, and the pawn is solidly guarded by the knight and the queen.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 Bg7.strategy: Completes Black's own fianchetto and puts the bishop on the long diagonal, aimed at White's queenside once the knight on f6 moves. Black keeps every pawn set-up open and can castle next, so the choice between challenging the centre at once and building a compact position stays with Black.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 d5.name: English Opening: Anglo-Indian Defence, Grünfeld Formation
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 d5.strategy: Strikes at c4 at once, before White has built a pawn centre. If White takes, Black's knight recaptures on an active central square and the bishop on g7 will bear on the long diagonal. A direct, respectable way to fight for equality.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 b6.strategy: Prepares the second fianchetto, with the bishop contesting the long diagonal and the e4 square. Black controls the centre from a distance rather than occupying it. Sound and flexible, but it delays the king's bishop and leaves the centre to White for now.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 c6.name: English Opening: Anglo-Indian Defence, Slav Formation
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 c6.strategy: Prepares to support a later central pawn thrust and keeps the queen's bishop free. It is solid but slow: a pawn move that develops no piece, so White gets time to build up and Black has to be patient before the centre can be challenged.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 b6 4.Bg2.strategy: Develops the bishop on the long diagonal and prepares castling. Both sides now have a fianchetto plan, and the bishop on g2 presses on the centre and the long diagonal that Black's queen's bishop wants to occupy.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 b6 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops the queen's knight toward d5 and e4, squares on the long diagonal Black's queen's bishop wants to use, and keeps the fianchetto in hand. White stays flexible about the pawn centre; the c-pawn is blocked, so the central plan runs through the d-pawn or a later e-pawn advance.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 b6 4.d4.strategy: Takes the centre before developing the bishop. It is sound, but the knight on f3 now stands in the line of Black's queen's bishop on the long diagonal, and White has to spend time on the bishop and the knight before the centre is secure.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 b6 4.Bg2 Bb7.strategy: Black develops the queen's bishop on the long diagonal and has the king's bishop still to place. 1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 b6 4.Bg2 Bg7.strategy: Completes the second fianchetto and clears the way for castling. Both bishops are wanted on the long diagonals, so the order costs nothing, and Black keeps every central plan open while White has the same choice.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 b6 4.Bg2 c5.strategy: Stakes a claim on d4 and takes queenside space, the b6-pawn supporting the advance. It is sound, but it commits the c-pawn and a queenside structure before the king is safe, and the bishops are still undeveloped.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 Bg7 4.Bg2.strategy: Completes the fianchetto: the bishop looks down the long diagonal and White can castle at once. Both sides now have the same king's-side set-up, and the fight is for the centre and the queenside rather than for development.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 Bg7 4.Nc3.strategy: Brings the queen's knight toward the centre, eyeing d5 and e4, and keeps the choice between a fianchetto and a classical pawn centre. The cost is the c-pawn's file, which the knight now blocks.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 Bg7 4.d4.strategy: Takes the centre at once, with the bishop's fianchetto still in hand. Black has to undermine the d4 pawn with pawn breaks and piece play, so the game turns on who controls the centre.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 Bg7 4.Bg2 O-O.strategy: Black castles and puts the king behind its fianchettoed bishop. It also frees a rook and keeps the choice of central plan open. Nothing is committed in the centre yet, so the game stays flexible for both sides.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 Bg7 4.Bg2 d6.strategy: Puts a pawn on d6 that guards c5 and e5 and opens the diagonal for the queen's bishop. A solid, flexible set-up that postpones the choice of central break until Black has seen what White does.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 Bg7 4.Bg2 c5.strategy: Mirrors White's c-pawn, claims d4 and takes queenside space before castling. Black gets a solid, symmetrical set-up without weaknesses and White decides whether to challenge in the centre.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 Bg7 4.Bg2 O-O 5.O.strategy: White follows suit and the two fianchetto set-ups are mirrored. Neither side has a pawn centre yet, so the next moves decide the character of the game: the side that takes space in the centre first sets the agenda.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 Bg7 4.Bg2 O-O 5.d.strategy: Seizes the centre with Black's king committed to the kingside. White's own king is well guarded behind the fianchetto, so the pawn centre is a real asset and Black must find counterplay against it rather than attack.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 Bg7 4.Bg2 O-O 5.N.strategy: Develops the queen's knight toward d5 and e4 and delays castling and the central decision. White keeps the choice between a quiet set-up and a central strike, at the cost of a knight on the c-file that blocks the c-pawn.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 Bg7 4.Bg2 O-O 5.O.strategy: Stakes a claim on d4 and takes queenside space, answering White's c-pawn with its own. A symmetrical set-up follows, in which Black has a solid position and no weaknesses, a good choice for a quiet middlegame.
